logline: A Mossad hacker-agent goes dark inside Tehran on a mission to disable an Iranian nuclear reactor - a survival thriller operating at the intersection of tradecraft, identity, and geopolitical terror.

renewal.note: Renewed for Season 4 at Apple TV+; Season 3 premiered globally January 9 2026 after a two-year delay due to the Gaza war and Iran - Israel conflict.

bollymeter.basis: 94% on Rotten Tomatoes from 18 critics; critics praised the show's genre efficiency and Niv Sultan's performance, while noting the premise required a certain suspension of tactical realism.

pull_quotes.text: Tehran is a taut and exciting spy thriller anchored by an electric performance from Niv Sultan.

seasons.review_body: Tehran's debut season solved an unusual problem: how to make a geopolitical spy thriller without turning its own geopolitics into propaganda. The show, originally produced for Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11 before Apple acquired international rights, keeps the Israel - Iran conflict as backdrop rather than argument. Tamar Ben David, a Mossad hacker who enters Tehran under cover, is required to improvise at every turn - and the show's writers gave her a city that felt lived-in and hostile in equal measure. The 94% RT score reflected critical appreciation for the procedural rigour and Sultan's performance. Audiences were slightly cooler (7.6 IMDb) but the show had built a global following by season's end.

episode_reviews.title: Tamar
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes Tamar's cover identity and the mission parameters while immediately complications arise - the operation that should be clinical becomes personal. The show's visual register is clean and procedural, more Le Carré than 24, and the opening hour earns its tension through logistics rather than action-movie shorthand.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Tamar walking through Tehran streets, navigating a city that looks ordinary and feels like a trap - the show's central visual metaphor, introduced without fanfare.

critic_note.text: Tehran launches with the assurance of a show that knows exactly what it is and how to do it.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 8
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale compresses the mission's endgame into an hour that functions as a sustained stress test. The show's intelligence about tradecraft pays off here - the climax is built on procedure, not coincidence, which makes the stakes feel earned. The ending opened the series to a second season without the artificiality of a manufactured cliffhanger.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The reactor facility sequence - the show does more with silence and bureaucratic precision than most thrillers manage with gunfire.

critic_note.text: A finale that respects its audience's intelligence as much as its protagonist's.

bollymeter.basis: 83% on Rotten Tomatoes; Glenn Close's addition raised the show's profile but critics noted a slightly less focused season compared to the debut run's clarity of mission.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 landed Glenn Close as a CIA operative intersecting with Tamar's continued off-grid existence, a casting move that generated visibility without quite generating the dramatic heat the show needed. Critics at 83% on RT found the season entertaining but noted that the central mystery was less elegantly structured than Season 1's single mission clarity. The Tamar-in-hiding premise required the show to find new engines of tension, and it found them - the romance with an Iranian dissident, the internecine intelligence politics - but the gears showed more than before. Audiences were consistent with Season 1, and the show won the International Emmy for Best Drama.
seasons.season_over_season: The addition of Glenn Close signals the show's ambition but the mission clarity of S1 is somewhat diffused.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes per early critical response; Hugh Laurie's addition as a South African nuclear inspector was widely praised, and critics noted the show had returned to the focused intensity of Season 1.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 finally premiered in January 2026 after a two-year delay driven by real-world events that made the show's subject matter genuinely sensitive. The delay, paradoxically, sharpened the show's impact: critics found the nuclear-inspector plotline featuring Hugh Laurie newly resonant in ways that could not have been planned. The 100% early RT score placed this among the show's best-received seasons. Laurie brings an academic's nervous precision to his role as an IAEA inspector whose access becomes the pivot of the Mossad operation. The show had found its second gear after Season 2's mid-run wobble.
seasons.season_over_season: A genuine return to form - the delay aged the show's ambitions rather than staling them.
